subject: Archaeology
title: Göbekli Tepe: The Temple Before Farming
description: One-minute skill: Göbekli Tepe: The Temple Before Farming.

hook.text: Hunter-gatherers in Turkey built a stone temple 11,600 years ago — 6,000 years before Stonehenge and before agriculture.

buildup.text: Göbekli Tepe has massive T-shaped pillars carved with lions, foxes, scorpions, and vultures. The largest weigh 10 tons.

discovery.text: Klaus Schmidt began excavating in 1995 and found multiple enclosures intentionally buried by their builders.

twist.text: It overturned the theory that farming came before religion. At Göbekli Tepe, belief came first.

climax.text: Only 5 percent of the site has been excavated. The rest lies buried, deliberately preserved by its original builders.

punchline.text: They built a temple before they grew crops.

quiz.question: How did Göbekli Tepe change our understanding of civilization?
options: It proved that agriculture was invented in Turkey, not the Fertile Crescent
It showed that religion and monumental building may have preceded farming
It demonstrated that stone tools were invented much earlier than believed

details.summary: Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, built around 9500 BCE, features massive carved stone pillars erected by hunter-gatherers before agriculture. It challenges the assumption that farming enabled monumental construction, suggesting that religious motivation may have driven the agricultural revolution itself.
details.whyItMatters: Göbekli Tepe inverted the conventional sequence of civilization: religion before agriculture, temples before villages. It suggests that the desire to gather for worship may have driven humans to settle and farm.
takeaways: Built around 9500 BCE by pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers
Massive carved stone pillars predate farming and pottery
It suggests religion may have driven the agricultural revolution

faq.question: Why is Göbekli Tepe so revolutionary?
faq.answer: Archaeologists assumed monumental construction required agricultural surplus to feed builders. Göbekli Tepe proves hunter-gatherers could organize complex construction projects. This inverts the accepted sequence: rather than farming enabling temples, temples may have motivated farming.

faq.question: What do the carved pillars at Göbekli Tepe depict?
faq.answer: T-shaped pillars up to 5.5 meters tall feature carved animals — foxes, lions, scorpions, vultures, snakes — and abstract human arms. The carvings suggest a rich symbolic world. The site appears to have been deliberately buried around 8000 BCE for unknown reasons.
